title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
what_it_does: Formalizes the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, validating LLM judges against human preferences and cataloguing judge failure modes (position, verbosity, self-enhancement bias).
key_results: GPT-4 judge matches human preferences with over 80% agreement (human-human level) while systematically exhibiting position and verbosity biases.
drawbacks: Almost entirely English-centric; bias analysis limited to a few coarse categories without linguistic dimensions.
gap_vs_ours: Does not examine language, script, or transliteration effects at all; we test whether identical content in Devanagari vs romanized Hindi receives different scores.

title: Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
what_it_does: Shows pairwise LLM evaluation is systematically vulnerable to positional bias (rankings hackable by reordering candidates); proposes a calibration framework.
key_results: Exploiting position alone makes Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries; calibration substantially improves alignment with humans.
drawbacks: Single bias type (position), English-only, small query set.
gap_vs_ours: Treats fairness as ordering robustness, not surface-form robustness; never asks whether the writing system of identical content shifts judge scores.

title: Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge
what_it_does: CALM: automated perturbation-based framework quantifying a taxonomy of 12 biases in LLM judges (position, verbosity, self-enhancement, authority, bandwagon, etc.).
key_results: Even advanced judges that look robust in aggregate show significant persistent biases on specific tasks; judge reliability is task-dependent.
drawbacks: The 12-bias taxonomy is built and measured on English data only; perturbations never vary language or orthography.
gap_vs_ours: Script/transliteration bias is absent from the taxonomy; our study adds an orthography-level bias axis.

title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
what_it_does: Isolates self-preference bias: judges (GPT-4, Llama 2) recognize their own outputs and inflate scores for them.
key_results: Linear correlation between self-recognition accuracy and self-preference strength; fine-tuning that increases self-recognition also increases self-preference (causal link).
gap_vs_ours: Shows judges favor familiar-looking text (their own style) but never tests familiarity at the writing-system level.

title: Are Large Language Model-based Evaluators the Solution to Scaling Up Multilingual Evaluation?
what_it_does: First large calibration study of GPT-4 as multilingual evaluator vs 20K human judgments across 3 tasks, 5 metrics, 8 languages including non-Latin scripts.
key_results: GPT-4 evaluators show systematic bias toward higher scores and poor calibration with native-speaker judgments, worst for lower-resource languages.
drawbacks: Each language evaluated only in its standard native orthography; one judge model.
gap_vs_ours: Includes Hindi in native script but never presents the same content in alternate scripts, so it cannot separate language bias from script bias.

title: PARIKSHA: A Large-Scale Investigation of Human-LLM Evaluator Agreement on Multilingual and Multi-Cultural Data
what_it_does: Compares ~90K human evaluations with 30K LLM-judge evaluations of 30 models across 10 Indic languages, pairwise and direct assessment.
key_results: Human-LLM agreement fair for pairwise but drops sharply for direct assessment, worst for Bengali and Odia; GPT-based evaluator shows self-bias.
drawbacks: Analyzes agreement per language as-is without controlled manipulation of any single factor.
gap_vs_ours: Script is a confound rather than a treatment; we hold Hindi content constant and vary only Devanagari vs Latin.

title: MM-Eval: A Multilingual Meta-Evaluation Benchmark for LLM-as-a-Judge and Reward Models
what_it_does: Multilingual meta-evaluation benchmark: 5 core subsets, 18 languages, plus a 122-language consistency subset stress-testing judges and reward models.
key_results: Evaluators strong in English are unfair and inconsistent on lower-resourced languages, tending to assign middling scores.
drawbacks: Measures per-language judge accuracy; does not manipulate orthographic form within a language.
gap_vs_ours: Its language-consistency axis stops at the language level; we extend consistency testing within one language to the script level.

title: How Reliable is Multilingual LLM-as-a-Judge?
what_it_does: Measures cross-lingual judgment consistency of five judge models across five tasks and 25 languages; proposes an ensemble strategy.
key_results: Only ~0.3 average Fleiss' Kappa consistency across languages, worst in low-resource languages; neither more multilingual data nor scale fixes it.
drawbacks: Consistency defined across translations between languages, conflating translation quality with judge behavior.
gap_vs_ours: Cannot attribute inconsistency to orthography because language and script co-vary; our transliteration design isolates script.

title: Lower-Resource, Higher Scores: Language Bias in LLM Evaluators
what_it_does: Audits multilingual LLM evaluators on semantically identical instruction-response pairs across 23 languages, measuring language-dependent score shifts.
key_results: Systematic cross-model score shifts, up to 43% acceptance-rate difference across languages; lower-resource languages scored MORE favorably; language identity predictive even after controlling for uncertainty.
drawbacks: Compares across languages in standard scripts only; translation-based pairs introduce noise.
gap_vs_ours: Closest methodological neighbour, but varies language rather than writing system; confirms the language axis can run OPPOSITE to expectations, motivating our script-only isolation.
